findings.title: Negative and zero amounts are now accepted
findings.description: The removed `if total <= 0: raise ValueError(...)` check is not replaced. `float("-5")` and `float("0")` parse successfully, so parse_money("-5") now returns -500 and parse_money("0") returns 0 instead of raising, silently allowing negative/zero expense amounts into the ledger. The removed test case for "-5" masks this regression.

findings.title: Floating-point rounding errors corrupt monetary values
findings.description: Using float() and `int(dollars * 100)` for currency is unsafe: many decimal amounts are not exactly representable in binary floating point (e.g. 19.99 * 100 can evaluate to 1998.9999999999998), and int() truncates rather than rounds, so parse_money can silently return the wrong number of cents for common, valid inputs. The previous regex+integer-arithmetic approach avoided this entirely.

findings.title: Excess fractional digits are silently truncated instead of rejected
findings.description: The old regex limited the fractional part to 1-2 digits and rejected anything else (e.g. "12.345" raised ValueError). The new implementation accepts "12.345" as float 12.345, multiplies to 1234.5 and truncates to 1234 cents, silently discarding a half-cent instead of signalling malformed input. This changes documented/tested behavior without the PR describing it as a behavior change.

findings.title: Non-ValueError exceptions can escape for inf/overflow inputs
findings.description: float("inf") or float("1e400") parse successfully (no ValueError raised by float()), but `int(dollars * 100)` on an infinite value raises OverflowError, not ValueError, which is not caught by the try/except and propagates uncontrolled, violating the function's documented contract of raising ValueError on malformed input.

findings.title: float() accepts formats the old parser rejected (scientific notation, underscores)
findings.description: Because parsing now delegates to Python's float(), strings like "1e3" or "1_000" are accepted as valid amounts (parsed as 1000.0), whereas the previous strict regex only accepted plain digits with an optional 1-2 digit fraction. This widens accepted input formats beyond what the docstring ("$12.50" style) and tests describe, which could let unexpected client input through.

findings.title: Regression tests for negative amounts and extra decimal digits were deleted, not updated
findings.description: The PR removes "-5" and "12.345" from the rejection test list instead of asserting the new (and arguably incorrect) behavior. This hides the negative/zero-amount regression and the silent-truncation regression described above, since no test exercises these inputs at all anymore.
